questions.question: If an array is declared as `int day[5] = {16, 2, 77};`, what value is stored in `day[3]`?
options: Undetermined garbage value
Causes a compilation error
questions.explanation: When initializing an array with fewer values than its declared length, C++ automatically fills the remaining elements with zero.

questions.question: Why does using `cin >> mybuffer;` fail when attempting to read a user's full name like "John Doe"?
options: The extraction operator >> only accepts numerical characters
The extraction operator >> treats spaces as delimiters and stops reading after 'John'
A character array cannot be passed to cin directly
The string must end with a semicolon to be accepted by cin
questions.explanation: The extraction operator >> treats any whitespace (including spaces and tabs) as a delimiter, capturing only the first word.

questions.question: What is the key difference between pass-by-value and pass-by-reference when passing an argument to a function?
options: Pass-by-reference works only with constant expressions, while pass-by-value works with variables
Pass-by-value passes the memory address, whereas pass-by-reference creates a local copy
Pass-by-value is only permitted for structures, while pass-by-reference is for basic types
Pass-by-value makes a copy so changes do not affect the original variable, whereas pass-by-reference modifies the caller's variable directly
questions.explanation: Pass-by-value copies the argument value into a local parameter, whereas pass-by-reference binds directly to the caller's variable.

questions.question: Where must parameters with default values be placed in a C++ function declaration?
options: At the end (right side) of the parameter list
At the beginning (left side) of the parameter list
In any order, provided parameter names are distinct
Alternating between standard parameters and default parameters
questions.explanation: In C++, all parameters with default arguments must always be positioned at the right side of the function declaration.

questions.question: Suppose `short *myshort;` points to memory address 2000. If `sizeof(short)` is 2 bytes, what address does `myshort` point to after executing `myshort++;`?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic increments by the size of the data type pointed to; adding 1 to a short pointer adds 2 bytes, yielding 2002.

questions.question: How does an array of character pointers (`char *name[5]`) optimize memory compared to a 2D array (`char names[5][20]`)?
options: It stores all characters in CPU registers instead of RAM
It converts strings into integers using atoi() automatically
It allocates only the exact length needed for each string plus '\0', eliminating wasted padding bytes
It prevents the compiler from allocating any memory until program termination
questions.explanation: A 2D char array allocates a fixed 20-byte block per row regardless of length, whereas an array of pointers points to strings sized to their actual contents.

questions.question: What happens if an `ofstream` object opens an existing file named "data.txt" with `open("data.txt", ios::out)`?
options: The existing contents of the file are discarded and overwritten
New output is automatically appended to existing content
The file is write-protected and opening fails
The file is automatically duplicated to a backup file
questions.explanation: Opening an existing file in `ios::out` mode discards all preexisting contents with no warning, leaving the file empty for new writes.

questions.question: In C++ file I/O, which pair of member functions is used to reposition and inspect the get pointer (input pointer)?
options: rewind() to reposition and fpos() to inspect
seekg() to reposition and tellg() to inspect
seekp() to reposition and tellp() to inspect
move() to reposition and locate() to inspect
questions.explanation: The get pointer (input file pointer) is moved using seekg() and its current byte offset is inspected using tellg().

questions.question: Why should data members of a class typically be declared `private` rather than `public`?
options: To reduce the memory footprint of each instantiated object
To allow global functions to modify the variables directly
To enforce data hiding and protect the object's internal state from unintended external modification
To allow the compiler to inline all member functions automatically
questions.explanation: Declaring data members private enforces data hiding, ensuring data can only be accessed or altered through controlled public methods.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between an accessor function and a mutator function in a class?
options: Accessors are always private, while mutators must be public
Accessors execute only during object destruction, while mutators execute during construction
Accessors work with classes, while mutators only work with structures
Accessors retrieve member values without modifying them, while mutators modify member values
questions.explanation: Accessor functions (often named get...) inspect private variables, whereas mutator functions (often named set...) update private variables.

questions.question: In C++, what happens when an array name without brackets is passed to a function such as `mult(firstarray, 3)`?
options: The entire array is duplicated by value onto the runtime stack
The array is passed by reference because the array identifier represents the address of its first element
A compilation error occurs because brackets are required in function calls
Only the first element of the array is passed as an integer
questions.explanation: Passing an array name passes the base address of the array, meaning modifications made inside the function directly alter the original array elements.

questions.question: What integer result is returned by `strcmp("apple", "banana")`?
options: A positive integer because 'banana' contains more letters
A negative integer because 'apple' is lexicographically less than 'banana'
Zero because both words are valid strings
The value 1 indicating a comparison error
questions.explanation: strcmp() returns a negative integer when the first string is lexicographically smaller than the second string ('a' comes before 'b').

questions.question: Why does declaring `int maximum(int x, y);` cause a compilation error in C++?
options: Prototypes must specify default argument values for all parameters
Parameter names in prototypes cannot be single characters
A data type is required for each individual parameter in the parameter list
The function identifier maximum is a reserved compiler keyword
questions.explanation: In C++, writing int x, y in a parameter list is a syntax error; every parameter must explicitly include its data type (e.g. int x, int y).

questions.question: What is the behavior of a local variable declared with the `static` keyword inside a function?
options: It retains its value across function calls and initializes only once during the first call
It can be accessed directly from any other function in the source file
It is allocated on the heap and requires manual deletion
It is destroyed and reallocated each time the function is invoked
questions.explanation: Static local variables persist in memory throughout program execution, retaining their values between calls and initializing only on the initial call.

questions.question: Why is the assignment statement `fp = &x;` illegal in C++ if `float *fp;` and `int x;`?
options: The pointer type does not match the data type of the variable whose address is being assigned
The ampersand operator cannot be applied to an integer variable
The variable x has not been initialized with a constant value
The identifier fp is reserved exclusively for file pointers
questions.explanation: Pointers in C++ are strongly typed; a float* cannot point to an int variable without an explicit type conversion or void*.

questions.question: Given `int data = 15; int *p1 = &data; int **p2 = &p1;`, which expression evaluates to the integer value 15?
options: *data
questions.explanation: p2 is a pointer to pointer p1. Dereferencing once (*p2) yields p1, and dereferencing twice (**p2) yields the value stored in data (15).

questions.question: Why is it unnecessary to `#include <iostream>` in a C++ program that already includes `<fstream>`?
options: The classes in <fstream> are derived from the classes in <iostream>, providing all its stream functions
<fstream> is a preprocessor macro that replaces all stream objects
The C++ standard prohibits including both headers in the same source file
<fstream> disables standard console input and output completely
questions.explanation: Because fstream is derived from iostream (which in turn derives from ios), including <fstream> automatically provides the full functionality of <iostream>.

questions.question: What is the effect of calling `indata.seekg(-1L, ios::end);` on an open input file stream?
options: It resets the get pointer back to byte 0
It moves the get pointer one byte past the end of the file
It deletes the last byte stored in the file
It positions the get pointer at the very last byte of the file
questions.explanation: Seeking with offset -1L relative to ios::end repositions the stream get pointer to point directly to the final byte of the file.

questions.question: In C++ inheritance terminology, what is a class that inherits attributes and methods from an existing class called?
options: A base class or parent class
A subclass, derived class, or child class
An abstract template class
A superclass or ancestor class
questions.explanation: A class that derives properties from another class is known as a subclass, derived class, or child class.

questions.question: What happens if a programmer defines a constructor with arguments for a class, does not define a default constructor, and then writes `SampleClass obj;`?
options: The program compiles but crashes upon running
The compiler generates an implicit default constructor automatically
The object's members are all initialized to nullptr
A compilation error occurs because no matching zero-argument constructor exists
questions.explanation: When any constructor is explicitly defined, the compiler ceases to provide a default constructor; declaring an object without arguments then causes a compilation error.

questions.question: Given two structure variables `store[44]` and `store[19]` of type `Company`, what does `store[44] = store[19];` do?
options: It copies all member values from store[19] into store[44]
It converts store[44] into a pointer pointing to store[19]
It swaps the memory addresses of store[44] and store[19]
It results in a syntax error because structures cannot be assigned with =
questions.explanation: In C++, complete structure variables of identical types can be assigned using =, which copies all member values from one structure to the other.

questions.question: Which `<cstdlib>` library function converts a character array storing numeric characters into a value of type int?
options: atof()
atol()
atoi()
itoa()
questions.explanation: The atoi() function parses an ASCII string of digits and returns its equivalent integer value.

questions.question: Why can two functions `int calc(int x)` and `double calc(int x)` NOT be overloaded in C++?
options: Function names in C++ must never share the same prefix
C++ requires overloaded functions to be declared in separate namespaces
Overloaded functions must differ in their parameter lists, not solely in their return types
Overloading is only permitted for functions that return void
questions.explanation: C++ determines which overloaded function to call based solely on parameter types and counts; differing only by return type is not allowed.

questions.question: What happens if a recursive function does not include a valid termination condition or fails to converge on it?
options: The compiler converts the recursion into an iterative while loop
The function automatically exits when local variables reach zero
The program returns 0 immediately without executing
The function calls itself indefinitely until the runtime stack overflows
questions.explanation: Without a base case, recursive calls continue allocating stack frames sequentially until the runtime stack exhausts available memory, causing stack overflow.

questions.question: Given `int arr[] = {11, 22, 33}; int *p = arr;`, what does `cout << *p++;` output and where does `p` point immediately afterward?
options: Outputs 22 and advances p to point to 33
Outputs 11 and advances p to point to 22
Outputs 11 and leaves p pointing to 11
Outputs 12 and leaves p pointing to 11
questions.explanation: Because post-increment (p++) has higher precedence than *, the original address pointing to 11 is dereferenced first, and p is then incremented to point to 22.

questions.question: Before dereferencing a void pointer `void *p;` storing the address of an integer variable, what action must be taken?
options: It must be assigned to nullptr first
It must be converted into a character array
It must be typecast to an int* before dereferencing
It must be freed using the delete operator
questions.explanation: Void pointers cannot be dereferenced directly because they lack type information; they must be explicitly typecast (e.g. static_cast<int*>(p)) first.

questions.question: Why does character reading using `cin.get(c)` differ from reading using `cin >> c`?
options: cin.get(c) reads all characters including spaces and newlines, whereas cin >> c skips whitespace
cin.get(c) requires a delimiter character parameter, while cin >> c does not
cin.get(c) only accepts uppercase characters, while cin >> c accepts any character
cin.get(c) reads data directly into the heap, while cin >> c uses the stack
questions.explanation: The extraction operator >> skips leading whitespace automatically, whereas get() reads the very next raw character without skipping blanks or newlines.

questions.question: In random-access file stream operations, what does the seek direction `ios::cur` indicate?
options: Positioning backward relative to the end of the file
Positioning relative to the current position of the pointer
Positioning relative to the beginning of the file
Resetting the file pointer to byte 0
questions.explanation: ios::cur specifies that the seek offset is calculated relative to the stream pointer's current location.

questions.question: What is the only fundamental distinction between a `class` and a `struct` in C++?
options: Struct members default to public, while class members default to private
Classes can be instantiated, while structures cannot
Classes allow member functions, while structures can only contain data members
Structures are stored in the heap, while classes are stored in registers
questions.explanation: In C++, both classes and structs can have data members and member functions; the distinction is that struct members default to public, while class members default to private.

questions.question: What is the purpose of constructor member initialization lists, such as `Coordinate(int xVal) : x(xVal) {}`?
options: To declare external prototypes for accessor functions
To override default private access control specifiers
To dynamically allocate memory on the heap before the constructor executes
To initialize member variables directly upon object instantiation before the constructor body executes
questions.explanation: Member initialization lists directly initialize member variables with values prior to the execution of the constructor's body statements.
